segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After the Sabbath, as it was dawning toward the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to look at the tomb.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And suddenly there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord came down from heaven, approached, rolled away the stone, and sat on it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing was white as snow.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For fear of him those keeping watch quaked and became like dead men.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the angel said to the women,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “As for you, do not be afraid, for I know that you are looking for Jesus, who was crucified.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: He is not here, for he has been raised, just as he said. Come, see the place where he was lying.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: Then go quickly and tell his disciples, ‘He has been raised from the dead, and look, he is going ahead of you to Galilee; there you will see him.’ Look, I have told you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they left the tomb quickly, with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And suddenly Jesus met them and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Greetings!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came up to him, took hold of his feet, and worshiped him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do not be afraid. Go and tell my brothers to go to Galilee, and there they will see me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While the women were on their way, some of the guard went into the city and told the chief priests everything that had happened.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After the chief priests had met with the elders and formed a plan, they gave the soldiers a large sum of money,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: telling them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Say, ‘His disciples came by night and stole him while we were asleep.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And if this comes to the governor’s ears, we will win him over and see that you have nothing to worry about.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they took the money and did as they were taught. And this story has been spread among Jews to this very day.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had told them to go.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they saw him, they worshiped him, but some doubted.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus came up and spoke to them, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Go, therefore, and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: teaching them to keep everything I have commanded you. And look, I am with you all the days, until the end of the age.”

notes.phrase: After the Sabbath, as it was dawning toward the first day of the week
notes.traditional: In the end of the sabbath, as it began to dawn toward the first day of the week
notes.note: The opening word can mean “late on” or “after”, and the verb rendered “dawning” can also be used of a new day “drawing on” at sunset, since the Jewish day began in the evening. A minority therefore place the visit on Saturday evening. Most scholars, comparing the other Gospels, take it as early Sunday morning, as here. “First day of the week” is literally “day one of the Sabbaths”, a Semitic way of counting days from the Sabbath.

notes.traditional: he is risen / he has risen
notes.note: The Greek verb is passive in form and can mean either “he was raised” (by God) or simply “he rose”. Many translations have “he has risen”. The passive is kept here because the New Testament regularly speaks of God raising Jesus, but both readings are grammatically sound.

The word is the ordinary Greek greeting of the day, as common as “hello”. Its literal sense is “rejoice”, which suits the scene, but a first-century hearer would have taken it first as an everyday greeting.

notes.traditional: if this come to the governor’s ears
notes.note: The Greek is literally “if this is heard before the governor”. That may mean simply that the report reaches him, or more specifically that the matter comes up for a formal hearing in his court. A Roman soldier who slept on watch faced severe punishment, which is why the priests promise to “win him over”, a phrase that may hint at a bribe.

The Greek has no “the”, so the statement is that the story circulated among Jewish people, not that it was the view of the people as a whole. Most translations supply the article. This is the only place where Matthew’s narrator uses the word outside the title “king of the Jews”.

The Greek can mean that some of the eleven doubted, or that they (all of them) worshiped and yet doubted. Most translations and scholars choose “some”. The verb means to waver or hesitate, not to disbelieve outright. Matthew uses it elsewhere only of Peter sinking on the water (14:31).

The same Greek word is translated “Gentiles” elsewhere in this translation, where it means the non-Jewish peoples. Here, with “all”, the scope is the whole world, and most scholars take it to include Israel. A minority read it as “all the Gentiles”, marking a turn from the mission to Israel alone in 10:5–6.

The Greek preposition is literally “into”. Some scholars think this signals transfer into the ownership or allegiance of the one named, while others note that “into” and “in” were often interchangeable in the Greek of the period. The traditional “in” is kept because the difference cannot be pressed with confidence.
Most translations have “always”. The Greek says “all the days”, a Semitic turn of phrase that suggests presence day by day up to the end, and it is kept here as written.

Older English versions have “the end of the world”. The Greek word is a time-word meaning an era, and the phrase reflects the Jewish contrast between the present age and the age to come. Most modern translations also have “age” here.

candidates.reason: The attention-marker occurs hundreds of times in narrative and speech, and translators vary between “behold”, “look”, “suddenly” and omission, so a policy is needed for uniformity.
The passive forms used of the resurrection can be rendered “was raised” or “rose”, and the choice should be uniform across the Gospels, Acts and Paul.
The plural here echoes the “silver pieces” paid to Judas in chapters 26–27, so “money” versus “silver” needs one decision to keep the link visible.
The verb covers guarding and obeying commandments across Matthew, John and Revelation, and translators vary between “keep”, “obey”, “observe” and “guard”.
It occurs only here and at Matthew 14:31, and “doubt” versus “hesitate” should match in both places.
